name: Spotify Mix
title: Spotify moved into mixing before anyone else — listeners were not following
subtitle: I found where listeners gave up, and rebuilt the workflow so it teaches as you mix.
tagline: The tools asked for DJ knowledge Spotify never taught, so users weren't set up to succeed. I found where listeners gave up, and rebuilt the workflow so it teaches as you mix.

phone.alt: The redesigned Spotify Mix edit-transition screen in motion

items: Mobile app, inside Spotify's design system
Quant survey · moderated testing · confidence scoring

text: Spotify Mix lets listeners craft real transitions between songs — matching keys, aligning BPM, shaping how tracks blend. In my survey, no one used Mix frequently; most had tried it once or twice and never went back.
I redesigned Mix inside Spotify's existing design system. Each step below starts from what Spotify ships today, then shows what I changed and why.

sections.heading: Smooth transitions required knowledge most listeners didn't have

blocks.text: Mixing well means understanding BPM compatibility, key matching, and what makes a transition sound intentional. In my survey, most respondents reported little or no familiarity with mixing terminology — and 9 of 11 who tried to learn the feature still felt confused afterward.

In moderated testing the pattern sharpened: multiple participants didn't realize Spotify even had a Smart Reorder feature moments after confidently reviewing the full interface, and participants repeatedly hunted for explanations whenever an unfamiliar concept appeared.

items.alt: Spotify's current mixed-playlist screen with BPM and key badges on every song row
items.title: Spotify today: every row carries BPM and key data, and nothing in the app explains what any of it means.

sections.heading: Make mixing approachable without dumbing it down

blocks.text: The redesign focused on reducing the cognitive load of mixing: simplifying decisions, providing guidance when users needed it, and keeping the full editing power in place for people who wanted it.
Two moments carried most of the confusion — editing a transition, and understanding what the system had already done for you. Those became the redesign's spine.

items.alt: Redesigned playlist screen: clean song rows with transition data moved out of the main list
items.title: The same playlist, refocused: BPM and key data move out of the main list and appear where you actually mix.

blocks.text: Many participants reported limited familiarity with mixing terminology, and primarily used presets when creating transitions. The redesigned editing experience keeps the dual-waveform view but promotes presets to the primary path, labels actions in plain language, and tucks advanced controls behind a deliberate step — accessible, not ambient.

blocks.title: Simplifying transition editing
blocks.caption: Spotify's edit screen opens onto raw waveforms and DJ controls. The redesign keeps the depth, but leads with presets and plain language — advanced controls sit one deliberate step away.

a.label: Spotify today
a.alt: Spotify's current edit-transition screen: raw waveforms, curves, and mixing controls all exposed at once

b.label: Redesign
b.alt: Redesigned edit-transition screen: dual waveform, blend curves, presets, plain-language actions

blocks.text: Smart Reorder — Spotify reordering your playlist for better transitions — was the feature participants loved most and found last. During testing, people simply couldn't find it, and once they did, the system's reasoning was invisible.
The redesign surfaces it as a first-class action and explains what changed and why, so the automation builds trust instead of suspicion.

blocks.title: Bringing Smart Reorder forward
blocks.caption: Today, Smart Reorder hides below the fold of Edit Playlist. The redesign makes it the first choice you see when you tap Mix.

a.label: Spotify today
a.alt: Spotify's current edit-playlist sheet, with Smart Reorder buried at the very bottom

b.label: Redesign
b.alt: Redesigned Mix sheet offering Smart Reorder as the first choice

sections.heading: Tap to learn more — teaching inside the moment

blocks.text: Simplifying alone doesn't build understanding. Wherever a concept like BPM or key compatibility appears, it's tappable: a short contextual explanation opens right where the question occurred, then gets out of the way.
In testing, participants successfully applied BPM and key concepts after receiving these contextual explanations — knowledge that a settings-buried help page had failed to transfer.

blocks.label: Spotify today
blocks.text: Spotify has nothing to compare here — there is no educational layer today

items.alt: 'Making mixing easy' sheet: match the key color, keep BPM close
items.title: Concepts explain themselves where they appear, and one sheet frames the two rules that matter: match the key color, keep BPM close.

sections.heading: Fixing a rough transition, step by step

blocks.text: The hardest task in testing was recovering from a transition that sounded bad. One participant put it plainly: "This is not as helpful… I have to try to figure it out on my own."

The redesign flags the hard blend directly on the timeline and offers a labeled fix — including adding a bridge song when two tracks simply don't want to meet. Directly labeled actions replaced guesswork.

blocks.title: Fixing a rough transition, step by step
blocks.caption: Spotify marks a clash with an orange badge and stops there. The redesign names the hard blend on the timeline and points at the fix.

a.label: Spotify today
a.alt: Spotify's current edit screen flagging a 125 bpm clash with a small orange badge

b.label: Redesign
b.alt: Redesign: the hard blend flagged and highlighted directly on the transition timeline

blocks.title: Fixing a rough transition, step by step
blocks.caption: When beat matching fails today, Spotify offers general tips and a Go back button. The redesign turns the dead end into an action: add a bridge song.

a.label: Spotify today
a.alt: Spotify's current dead end: 'Beat matching is not possible between some tracks', with a Go back button

b.label: Redesign
b.alt: Redesign: the add-a-bridge-song flow suggesting tracks that smooth the transition

blocks.note: All 11 participants preferred the redesign over Spotify’s current experience.

sections.heading: Design for different levels of involvement

blocks.text: Across usability testing, participants consistently rated the redesign higher than Spotify's current experience for confidence and understanding — average confidence moved from 2.6 to 3.7 out of 5, and every participant preferred the redesign.

The deeper lesson: some users wanted quick answers, others wanted detailed control. The redesign works because it serves both from the same screens — high-level clarity by default, depth one deliberate tap away.
